column2: Keep the Fast of the Prophets

For one month the faithful of the Prophets take neither food nor water while the sun is in the sky, and break the fast each night before the Holy Flame. A ruler who keeps it is cleansed of luxury and honoured by the scholars.
Kept the Fast of the Prophets
This character has kept the Fast of the Prophets and is held in high regard by the scholars.
The Fast of the Prophets begins
The Fast of the Prophets

The new moon has risen over the desert and the scholars have cried it from the towers: the Fast of the Prophets has begun. From first light to sunset no food or water shall pass my lips. Each night the Holy Flame is fed and the fast is broken with dates and milk, as the Prophets broke it when they wandered the sands. Ahgriman whispers loudest to the hungry. I must not listen.
In the name of Ormazd, I fast.

The scholars remind me that the Prophets showed mercy in the holy month, and that a ruler who fasts while men rot in his dungeons fasts for nothing. My prisoners wait in the dark below, and the whole court watches to see what I will do.
Open the cells. Let them go in the name of Ormazd.
Mercy is for the Prophets. They stay where they are.
In the souk the poor gather each evening at the palace gate, waiting for the alms the faithful owe in the holy month. My steward asks how much he should give them.
Open the treasury. No one goes hungry at night in my city.
The poor will be poor whatever I give them.

The night prayers of the holy month go on until dawn. The scholars chant the words of the Prophets before the Holy Flame, and every pious ruler is expected to kneel among them. My knees ache and my eyes are heavy.
I will pray until the sun rises.
Let the scholars pray. I am going to bed.
The days of hunger and thirst have taken their toll. My head swims in the heat of the afternoon and my hands shake. The physicians say my body is too weak for the fast and beg me to eat.
The physicians are right. I will end the fast.
The Prophets endured worse. I will go on.

I would not listen and now I cannot rise from my bed. The fever has burned the strength out of me, and the physicians whisper that I will never be whole again. The scholars call it a holy sacrifice. I call it a hard bargain.
Ormazd asked much of me, and I gave it.
I had thought hunger would make me weak, but it has made me clear. Each day without food teaches my body to obey me. I do not think I shall ever eat as I once did.
A ruler must first rule himself.
Every night of the fast I have watched the poor at my gate break their own fast on nothing but bread and water. I find I cannot sit at my table without thinking of them.
What I have is a gift. I will give it on.

A stranger sat among the guests at tonight's fast-breaking. No one remembers letting him in. When the lamps burned low he smiled at me with a mouth full of smoke, and I knew him for what he was: a djinn of the deep desert. He bowed and spoke softly. The fast is long and the night is short, he said, and he has gold and secrets for one who would set the Prophets aside for a single hour.
Begone, spirit, in the name of Ormazd!
Gold, then. One hour is a small price.
Teach me what the Prophets will not.
Riders have come with news of war. A ruler cannot lead men into battle on an empty stomach, and the scholars agree that the Prophets themselves set the fast aside when the sword was drawn.
The fast must wait. To war!
I have fallen ill, and the physicians forbid me to fast any longer. The scholars say there is no shame in it, for the Prophets ask nothing of the sick.
Then I must end the fast.

The holy month is nearly over. Custom asks that a lord break the last fast with a great feast for the vassals, with lamb roasted over the coals, sherbet cooled with mountain snow, and dancers from the south. It will not be cheap.
Send the invitations. Let all Araby see my generosity.
A quiet supper will do.
Your vassals are invited to the fast-breaking feast

Peace and the blessings of Ormazd upon you.

The holy month draws to a close, and I would break the last fast with those who serve me. Come to my palace and share my table, as the faithful have always done.

[From.GetTitledFirstName]
I will come.
I have better things to do.
Your liege is told you will not come

Peace upon you.

I regret that I cannot attend your feast. My own affairs keep me away.

[From.GetTitledFirstName]
An empty seat. I will remember it.
The feast is held

The last fast of the holy month is broken in the great hall. The lamps burn until dawn, the musicians never tire, and my vassals eat and drink their fill. Those who came will not soon forget my hospitality.
A fine end to a holy month.
You attend the feast
My liege's feast was everything they said it would be. I ate until I could eat no more, and the dancers were a wonder.
A generous liege, truly.
At the end of the holy month it is the custom to give gifts to one's household. [Root.Spouse.GetFirstName] will be expecting something fine.
A gift of silk and gold.
I have given enough this month.
At the end of the holy month it is the custom to give gifts to one's household, and my wives will each be watching to see what the others receive. Whatever I give, someone will be jealous.
Something fine for my first wife, trinkets for the rest.
Equal gifts for all of them, whatever the cost.
Nothing for anyone. Let them squabble.
Just a few dates. Just a handful of honeyed almonds, at noon, behind a closed door. No one will see. The Prophets will surely forgive a hungry man.
Delicious.
The holy month forbids the pleasures of the flesh while the sun is up. The sun is up, but the curtains are thick and the harem is cool and quiet.
The scholars need not know.
My servant fills my water jar each night. Today I had him fill it with the red wine of Tilea instead. I sip it all afternoon, and no one at court is the wiser.
Holy month indeed.
The alms for the poor pass through my treasury on their way to the gate. Somehow the purse that leaves is lighter than the purse that came in.
The poor will never miss it.
I kneel with the scholars, I say the words, and I feel nothing at all. The Prophets are silent and so is Ormazd. Perhaps they always were.
I go through the motions.
The fast ends

The holy month is over. The scholars call it from the towers, and across the city the faithful light lamps and break their fast together. Whatever I have gained or lost in these weeks, the Fast of the Prophets is done for this year.
Praise to Ormazd and the Prophets.
Hold the Night of a Thousand Lamps

In autumn the faithful of Ormazd light a thousand lamps from the Holy Flame to drive back the long nights of Ahgriman. Hold a month of feasting, invite your vassals and fill your palace with the wonders of the souk.
Holding the Night of a Thousand Lamps
This character is hosting the Night of a Thousand Lamps.
The palace servants are already hanging brass lamps from every arch and balcony. The Night of a Thousand Lamps approaches, and every vassal of mine must be invited to share it.
Send out the invitations.
Your vassals are invited to the Night of a Thousand Lamps

Peace and the light of Ormazd upon you.

The nights grow long and Ahgriman's darkness creeps closer, so we shall light a thousand lamps against it, as the faithful always have. Come to my palace and feast with me. The souk promises wonders this year.

[From.GetTitledFirstName]
I will come.
I must decline.
Your liege is told you will not come

Peace upon you.

I regret that I cannot attend your feast this year.

[From.GetTitledFirstName]
Then sit in the dark.

It is the custom on the Night of a Thousand Lamps to give a gift to the one you love. The goldsmiths and silk merchants of the souk have been at my door all week. What shall I give [Root.Spouse.GetFirstName]?
Rubies and silk, the finest in the souk.
A small token will do.
Nothing. The lamps are gift enough.
The rubies go to my lover instead.
[Root.Spouse.GetFirstName] opened the casket and gasped at the rubies. That night the lamps burned late in our chambers.
[Root.Spouse.GetFirstName] smiled politely at my little gift and thanked me. It was enough, I think.
[Root.Spouse.GetFirstName] waited all evening for a gift that never came, and has hardly spoken to me since.
My lover wept with joy over the rubies. Unfortunately, [Root.Spouse.GetFirstName] has heard where they went, and now no lamp in the palace burns as hot as my spouse's temper.
So it goes.

The Night of a Thousand Lamps has begun. Lamps hang from every arch, the courtyards are strewn with rose petals, and the cooks have been roasting lamb since dawn. The merchants of the souk have sent their best entertainers, and the scholars are already preparing the fire-temple for the lighting of the lamps.
Let the feast begin!
The Lighting of the Lamps

At sunset we go in procession to the fire-temple, where the scholars feed the Holy Flame with cedar and incense. One by one, a thousand lamps are lit from it and carried out into the city, until every roof and window glows and the night of Ahgriman is driven back for another year. Even the hardest faces in my court are wet with tears.
The light of Ormazd endures.
The feast is over. The lamps burn low and my guests ride home with full bellies and tales of wonders to tell. It will be remembered as a fine Night of Lamps.
The feast is over, and I would rather forget it. Between the disasters and the indignities, my guests will be telling stories about this Night of Lamps for years, and not the kind I want.
Until next year.
The Night of a Thousand Lamps is over and it is time to ride home. My liege's feast was a wonder.
The Night of a Thousand Lamps is over and I cannot leave quickly enough. I shall have nightmares about this feast.

A snake charmer from the souk sits cross-legged before the high table and plays a reedy tune on his pipe. Out of the basket rises a great black cobra, swaying with the music, its hood spread wide. The guests hold their breath.
Remarkable.
The charmer misses a note. The cobra drops out of its basket and slithers away under the tables, and the hall erupts in screams.
Somebody catch it!
The cobra is found at last, coiled peacefully in a guest's lap. It takes the charmer half an hour to coax it back into its basket, while the guest sits frozen as a statue.
The poor soul.
I sat with a cobra in my lap for half an hour while that fool of a charmer played his pipe at it. I could feel it breathing. I shall never forget the feel of it.
I need a drink. Several drinks.
The cobra was found too late. It had bitten one of my guests, who died in agony before the physicians could arrive. The charmer has fled the city.
A terrible night.
Before anyone else could move, one of my guests caught the cobra behind the head and dashed its brains out against a pillar. The hall burst into applause.
I killed the cobra with my bare hands in front of the whole court. They will be talking about this for years.
It was nothing.

Among the dancers tonight is one I cannot stop watching. Veiled in silk the colour of flame, the dancer moves like smoke and seems to glow in the lamplight. No one at the table knows where the dancer came from.
Have the dancer brought to me.
Let the dancer dance.

Up close the dancer is even more beautiful, with golden eyes that hold the light of the lamps. The dancer leans close and whispers that there is a garden behind the palace where the lamps cannot reach.
Show me this garden.
No. Not tonight.

I woke at dawn in the garden, alone, with the scent of smoke and jasmine on my skin. No one saw the dancer leave, the troupe swears they never hired anyone like that, and the guards at the gate saw nothing. The old women of the palace whisper that the djinn come to the lamp-feasts every year, looking for mortals foolish enough to follow them.
Whatever it was, it was worth it.
The Conjurer

A conjurer with a forked beard puts a boy into a wicker basket and runs it through with a sword, again and again. When he opens the basket it is empty, and the boy comes laughing through the doors at the far end of the hall.
How did he do it?
Sorcery! Guards, seize him!
The conjurer sets three brass cups on the table and hides a pearl under one of them. His hands blur as he moves the cups around, then he bows and asks me to choose.
The left cup.
The middle cup.
The right cup.
The cup is empty. The conjurer lifts the other two, and the pearl is under neither of them. He reaches behind my ear and produces it with a flourish while the guests roar with laughter.
Well played, conjurer.
You cheated, you dog!
It was up your sleeve the whole time.

The conjurer unrolls a threadbare carpet, sits on it cross-legged and claps his hands. Slowly the carpet rises from the floor, hangs above the astonished guests, glides once around the hall and settles again at my feet. They say the true carpets of Araby can fly from Copher to Lashiek in a night.
Wonderful!
I can see the wires.

A merchant from the Southlands has brought a troupe of trained monkeys to perform. They perform for exactly as long as it takes them to notice the food. Then they are everywhere: on the tables, in the dishes, in the guests' hair, shrieking and throwing fruit.
This is a disgrace!
Hand me my bow.
Catch one. Let me show you what happens to thieves.
Look, it likes me!

A procession has arrived from Araby: drummers, dancers, slaves bearing gifts, and at its head, swaying under a canopy of gold, an elephant as white as milk. The ambassador of [elephant_giver.GetTitledName] bows low and announces that the Sultan, in his boundless friendship, presents this marvel to me. No one has ever refused a gift from a Sultan and stayed his friend.
I am honoured beyond words.
Take your elephant and go home.

The ambassador lingers to make sure the white elephant is properly housed. In Araby, he explains, such a beast lives in a palace of its own, with marble floors, fountains and servants to fan it. Anything less would insult the Sultan.
Build it a marble stable, then.
It is an animal. The old barn will do.
Every quack and hedge-wizard in my city is selling the white elephant's dung as a cure for gout, baldness and barren wives. My grooms have been caught selling it by the bucket at the back gate.
Flog the quacks and the grooms with them.
Give it to the poor to manure their fields.
If it sells, tax it.
The white elephant is bored. Last night it smashed its way through the stable walls, ate the roof thatch and trampled the stable-master's garden. The repairs will be expensive.
Rebuild the stable.
Send it back to the Sultan.
Sell it to a travelling menagerie.
This beast has to die.
The white elephant has escaped again and is rampaging through the market, trumpeting at every stall and chasing the city's mules, apparently looking for a mate. The merchants are furious.
Catch it gently and lead it home.
Open the gates and let it go.
Butcher it and sell the ivory.
It must die. Quietly.
After months of chaos the white elephant has finally settled into its new home. It eats from the children's hands and trumpets when I visit. Word of its contentment has even reached the Sultan.
A fine beast, after all.
The white elephant has to go, but the Sultan must never learn that it died at my hands. How is it to be done?
Poison in its fodder.
Stop feeding it.
An accident on the cliff road.
Lances. I will not sneak about in my own stables.
The white elephant is dead, and the physicians agree it was a sudden fever brought on by our cold climate. I have sent a letter of deepest sorrow to the Sultan.
Such a tragedy.
Somehow the Sultan has learned exactly how the white elephant died. His ambassador left my court this morning without a word, and the story is being told in every bazaar from Copher to Lashiek.
It was only an elephant!
A war elephant has broken its chains in the capital and is rampaging through the streets, crushing carts and stalls and anyone too slow to get out of its way. The mahouts cannot calm it.
Soldiers! Bring it down!
Take it alive. It cost a fortune.
The soldiers brought the elephant down at last, but only after a long and bloody hour of spears, arrows and screaming in the middle of the market. The people will not forget it soon.
An ugly business.
My archers brought the elephant down with a single volley before it could do any more harm. The people cheer their protectors in the streets.
Well done.
The ropes snapped and the elephant broke free, trampling three men to death before it vanished into the desert. The families of the dead are demanding blood money.
Pay them.
The mahouts and a few brave soldiers roped the elephant at last and led it, exhausted, back to its stall. The people praise the courage of my men.
Back to work, beast.

My servants are whispering about a holy man who has come up the Ivory Road and taken a pitch in the great souk. They say he sits cross-legged in the air, a hand's breadth above his mat, and has not touched the ground in three days. Half the city has gone to gape at him.
I must see this for myself.
Conjurers' tricks. I have better things to do.

The crowd parts for me. The fakir is a wizened, sun-blackened man in a loincloth, ash smeared over his brow, and he sits in the air as if on a cushion. His eyes are closed. He does not seem to know I am here, or care.

column1: The merchants swear he is touched by the djinn. A Tilean spice trader at my elbow mutters that it is a trick with a hidden rod.

column2: A marvel of the East. Let him be.
Leave a purse of gold at his feet.
Prod him with my staff and see what happens.
Push him off. Let us see him float then.
I poke the fakir in the ribs. He sways in the air like a lamp on a chain, then settles again. His eyes stay shut. The crowd has gone very quiet.
Harder this time.
Enough. I walk away.
Off with him!
I jab him again, harder. He drifts sideways a full arm's length, then glides back to his mat as if nothing had happened, and never once opens his eyes.

column1: I have proven nothing except that I am the sort of ruler who pokes holy men in the market. The crowd mutters as I leave.

column2: At least they will remember who rules here.
I put my boot to him and shove with all my weight. He tumbles off his mat and lands in the dust with a thud and a yelp, very much like any other old man.

column1: The crowd gasps, then howls. Some say I have unmasked a fraud. More say I have laid hands on a saint, and that the djinn will not forget it.

column2: Floating men. Hah. There is no magic in this world but gold and steel.

I leave the fakir hanging in the air and walk back to the palace through the spice stalls. All evening the question gnaws at me. A rod? A djinn? The Winds of Magic blowing through a starving old man? I will never know.
Some mysteries are better left alone.

A caravan from far Cathay has come in over the mountains, and with it a band of shaven-headed monks in saffron robes who serve, they say, the Celestial Dragon Emperor himself. At dawn they go through their forms in the caravanserai yard, striking and kicking and leaping in perfect silence, and I am told they can break a plank with a bare hand and catch an arrow in flight.

column1: Their leader has asked, through an interpreter, for leave to stay a season before going on.

column2: Stay, and teach my guards how it is done.
Warriors who pretend to be priests? Spies of the Dragon Emperor, every one.

Two brothers from Tilea are waiting in my audience hall, a pair of Remas merchants with a young nephew in tow. They have come all the way down the coast and across the desert, and they mean to go further still, along the Ivory Road to the court of the Dragon Emperor in Cathay. They beg a moment of my time.
Let them speak.
I have no time for wandering pedlars.

The elder brother bows low. They carry letters for the Emperor of Cathay, he says, and hope to open a road for silk, jade and spice that would make every city along it rich. But the road is long, the mountains are cruel, and the Dark Lands between are full of greenskins and worse. Any help I could give would be remembered, he swears, and repaid.
A letter of safe passage and a modest purse.
Camels, guards and gold. Let all Cathay hear of my generosity.
I wish them luck. Nothing more.
The Tileans load their camels at first light and ride out of the east gate with the morning caravan. The nephew turns in the saddle to wave. Who knows if any of them will come back alive.
Safe roads.
The Tileans bow stiffly and take their leave. I hear they found a Cathayan jade trader willing to let them join his caravan for a ruinous price.
Their business, not mine.

A dusty caravan has come in from the East, and at its head ride the Tilean brothers, grey and leathery now, with the nephew grown into a man. They have spent years at the court of the Dragon Emperor, they tell me, and seen cities of jade, paper money, rockets that burst into flowers of fire, and a wall that has no end. They did not forget who sent them on their way. Their gifts are laid out before my throne: bolts of silk, porcelain, tea, and books in a script no one here can read.
Tell me everything.
Make the Pilgrimage to Ind

Far beyond the edge of the known world, where the Spice Route ends, lies the Kingdom of Ind, the land of a thousand gods. Its holy places draw pilgrims of every faith in the East. The journey takes the better part of a year, and not everyone comes back.
You will be away from your realm for about nine months.
On the Road to Ind
This character is far away on the pilgrimage to the holy places of Ind.
Pilgrim of Ind
This character has made the long pilgrimage to the holy places of Ind and come home wiser for it.
The camels are loaded, the guides are paid, and the caravan master says the Spice Route is open as far as the Sentinels and beyond. Where in Ind shall I go?

column1: The Temple of the Thousand Arms rises over the temple-city on the Sacred River, and its priests are said to know the answer to every question. The Tiger Shrine lies deep in the southern jungles, where the striped beasts walk free among the worshippers and only the brave may enter. On the burning ghats of the Sacred River the dead of Ind are given to the flames day and night, and the sick come to bathe and be healed.

column2: The Temple of the Thousand Arms.
The Tiger Shrine in the jungle.
The burning ghats of the Sacred River.
On second thoughts, I will stay at home.

The monsoon has come early. For days the rain has fallen in sheets, the road has turned to a river of red mud, and the caravan is stuck in a village of stilt houses while the streams rise around us. The guides say it could last weeks. The pilgrims in the next hut are already talking of wading on.
We wait. The gods will not hurry the rain.
Into the flood. My faith will carry me.

The rains failed this year. The plain is cracked like an old pot, the wells along the road are dry or full of dead things, and our water skins are half empty. A band of barefoot pilgrims, an old woman among them, follows our caravan with their tongues swollen in their mouths.
Share what we have.
Our water is for us.

The jungle closed over the road three days ago. Since then we have seen nothing but vines, monkeys and green twilight, and this morning the guide admitted, very quietly, that he is no longer sure where we are.
Keep following the guide.
The guide may lead you in circles until your supplies run low.
I will find the way by the stars myself.
Halt, and pray for a sign.

Where the road crosses a ravine, a gang of armed men waits on the bridge. Their leader wears a turban set with a great false ruby and calls himself the Rajah of the Ravine. He is very polite. Every pilgrim who crosses his bridge, he explains, pays his toll, and those who do not pay go into the ravine.
Pay the toll.
Draw steel and clear the bridge!
Flatter the rajah and talk our way across.

There is a man-eater on this stretch of the road. Two porters have vanished from the camp in as many nights, and last night I heard it myself, a deep coughing grunt in the dark just beyond the firelight. The porters will not go on unless something is done.
Give me a spear. I will face it.
Build up the fires and pray till dawn.

A courier has caught up with the caravan carrying letters from home, half a year old. There is trouble with the harvest, a quarrel among my vassals, and rumours at court that I have died on the road. I am very far from all of it.
My steward will manage. I trust him.
I write back long letters, every night.
Wherever the caravan halts, the poor of Ind come to it: lepers, cripples, widows, children with huge eyes and arms like sticks. They do not beg loudly. They only sit at the edge of the camp and wait.
Give them alms, all of them.
We cannot feed every beggar in Ind.

Two travellers have joined the caravan. One is a naked holy man smeared in ash, who has walked from the far north and talks all night of the thousand gods. The other is a fat spice merchant from the coast, who talks all night of prices. Both are good company, in their way.
I listen to the holy man.
I listen to the merchant.

I woke this morning shaking with fever, my sheets soaked through. The caravan's healer, a toothless old woman, says it is the jungle sickness and that she has a brew for it. It smells like a dead dog.
I will rest until it passes.
Give me the brew.

The road passes through a city of marble palaces and gilded domes, where painted elephants carry noblemen through streets strewn with flowers and the bazaars sell silks, jewels and spices no one at home has even heard of. The local rajah has heard that a foreign lord is passing, and invites me to his court.
I will pay my respects to the rajah.
A day in the bazaars, then on.
A pilgrim has no time for palaces.
The Holy Place

After so many months on the road I have reached the Temple of the Thousand Arms. It rises over the river like a mountain carved by giants, every inch of it crowded with statues of gods and demons, dancers, beasts and kings. The great idol inside has a thousand arms, and in each hand it holds a different gift. Incense hangs in the air so thick I can taste it, and the chanting of the priests never stops.

After so many months on the road I have reached the Tiger Shrine. It lies in a clearing deep in the jungle, a ruin of green stone half swallowed by roots. Tigers lie sleeping on the temple steps and in the shade of the courtyards, and the priests walk among them as if they were house cats. The pilgrims who come here enter barefoot and unarmed, and the priests say that the tigers know the hearts of those who pass.

After so many months on the road I have reached the burning ghats. Broad stone steps run down into the brown Sacred River for miles, and on every step the dead of Ind are burning on their pyres while their families sing. The sick bathe beside the ash in the shallows, the holy men sit naked in the smoke, and the river carries everything away to the sea.
I have arrived.

The priests of the temple have let me sit at their debates. They argue for days on end about the nature of the gods, the soul and the world, from a thousand books written in a script older than any kingdom I know. I understand perhaps one word in ten. But that one word is enough to change how I see my own faith.
There is so much more to learn.

On the third night, as I knelt in the smoke and the chanting, the world fell away. I saw my god as I have never seen him, and I knew, without any doubt at all, that I am seen and known. When I came back to myself the sun was up and the priests were watching me with great respect.
I have been touched by the divine.

The holy place is a fairground. Touts drag pilgrims by the sleeve to buy charms, the priests want a coin for every prayer, and the famous wonders are smaller and dirtier than the stories. I came all this way for this?
What a waste of a year.

Pilgrims from every corner of the East are here: shaven monks from Cathay, Arabyan merchants, Indish princes, wild hill tribesmen, even a pale scholar from the Old World who says he walked all the way. Each one is certain his own gods are the true ones, and each of them is kind to me.
The world is wider than I knew.
Here no one knows me, no one watches me, and the dancing girls of the temple are said to be the most beautiful in the world. My courtiers are half a year's journey away.
When in Ind...
I did not come all this way for that.

An old priest saw me coughing and led me down to the water. He washed me in the holy river, pressed a paste of ash and herbs to my chest and sang over me for an hour. The next morning I woke without fever for the first time in weeks.
It is a miracle.
Behind the holy places are the houses where the pilgrims drink soma, the milky drink of the gods, and dream with their eyes open. I only meant to try a cup. That was some days ago, I think.
Just one more cup.
Enough. I must get out of here.

Before the inner sanctuary lies a walled garden full of tigers. The priests say that a pilgrim who walks through it to the altar, unarmed and unafraid, is blessed by the gods with the courage of the tiger. Those the tigers judge unworthy are not blessed. They point to the bones by the wall.
Open the gate.
I will watch from here.

A holy man of the ghats, his body grey with the ash of the dead, invited me to sit with him by the pyres through the night. As the fires burned down he told me that the dead are not gone, only passing on, and pointed to faces in the smoke. I am almost sure I saw my own father among them.
I will sit with the dead until dawn.
I turn away from the smoke.

A messenger in cloth of gold came to my lodgings today with an invitation from the Maharajah who rules this land. He received me in a hall of mirrors and was so charmed to meet a foreign lord who had come so far for the gods that he has made me a gift: a herd of his war elephants, with their mahouts and spearmen, to march home with me.
I will lead them home in triumph!
A herd of war elephants (30 elephants and 120 light infantry) joins your army at half the usual upkeep.
I could never feed them. Thank him for the honour.

After nine months on the road I am home again, thinner, sun-blackened and older, with a sack of holy ash, a head full of stories and a peace in my heart I did not have before. The whole court has come out to greet me.
After nine months on the road I am home again, thinner, poorer, and none the wiser. The court has come out to greet me. I wish they had not.
It was worth every mile.
Never again.

On my last day at the temple the eldest of the priests came to my lodging with a bundle wrapped in saffron cloth. Inside were a hundred palm leaves covered in tiny script and bound between boards of sandalwood: a copy of the temple's scripture, made by his own hand. Few foreigners, he said, had listened as I had listened.
I will treasure it all my life.

When I came out of the tigers' garden the priests of the shrine were waiting for me at the gate. They threw a great striped skin over my shoulders, the pelt of a tiger that had lived to a great age in the shrine, and said that the tigers had judged me and found me worthy to wear it.
I will wear it into battle.

At dawn the holy man of the ghats led me down the steps into the brown water, past the ashes of the dead, until it reached my chest. He pushed my head under three times and sang over me in a language I did not know. When I came up the sun was rising over the river, and I have never felt so alive.
The river has blessed me.
Scripture of the Thousand Arms

A hundred palm leaves of tiny script bound between boards of sandalwood, copied by a priest of the Temple of the Thousand Arms in Ind. It holds the teachings of the temple on the thousand gods and the nature of the soul.
Mantle of the Tiger Shrine
The striped skin of a great tiger that lived out its days at the Tiger Shrine in the jungles of Ind, given by its priests to a pilgrim the tigers judged worthy.
Blessed by the Sacred River
This character was bathed in the Sacred River of Ind at the burning ghats and blessed by its holy men.
